patient.name: Kofi Mensah
patient.complaint: Four days of fever, cough and red eyes; a rash appeared this morning
background: MMR not given: parents declined at 12 months
Baby sister Ama, 5 months old, at home

diagnosis.exam: Expect a vignette of a classic infection (fever and rash, purpuric rash, whooping cough, cavitating TB) where you must recognise the disease and know it is notifiable, and how fast: immediately or within 3 days.

points: Runny nose, dry cough and **red, watery eyes**.
This morning a blotchy red rash began **behind his ears**.
Now spreading down his face and trunk.

steps.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.r: Cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, high fever, then a rash starting behind the ears in an unvaccinated child: **measles**.

steps.lead: Kofi's measles is one of the classic **notifiable diseases**: the law says it must be reported to public health.

points: Inside his cheeks: tiny white spots on a red base (**Koplik spots**).
His sister Ama, 5 months, came to the appointment too.
The GP asks: is this notifiable, and how fast?

steps.lead: Measles is in the **urgently notifiable** group with meningococcal meningitis, cholera and rabies: Kofi's GP must act **today**, not within 3 days.

steps.title: How fast must you notify?
head: Category
Examples
Deadline
rows: HIV, syphilis, herpes simplex, ophthalmia neonatorum

visual.title: Notification deadline (hours from suspicion)
visual.label: Kofi: measles, now
visual.caption: Urgent diseases are phoned through at once; routine ones within 72 hours.

steps.lead: The notes' exam clue is Kofi exactly: **fever, rash, generally unwell** means think measles and notify immediately.

steps.text: **HIV** is monitored but **not** legally notifiable, and neither are syphilis or herpes simplex. They are classic 'which is notifiable?' distractors.
Notification is triggered by **clinical suspicion**. Kofi's GP does not need a positive test to report him.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate next step?' where the answer is to notify now on clinical suspicion, with confirmatory samples (PCR, serology, blood cultures) sent alongside, never instead.

steps.q: Kofi's GP sends an oral fluid swab. When should she notify?
o: Only if a second case appears
steps.r: Notify on **suspicion**. Waiting days for results loses the window for protecting contacts.

steps.lead: Kofi's diagnosis is made by the GP's **clinical judgement plus formal notification**: no lab result is needed first.

steps.title: Suspicion to confirmation
nodes: Phone the local health protection team now
Send samples: oral fluid PCR / IgM, or blood
Lab confirms and also reports the organism
steps.caption: Notification and testing run in parallel, not in sequence.

steps.lead: Kofi's oral fluid swab and serology are **confirmatory** tests, sent after he has already been notified.

steps.title: Kofi's results (day 3)
steps.text: Confirmation arrives 3 days later: by then contacts must already have been protected.

visual.title: Antibody response after rash onset
visual.caption: IgM can still be negative in the first days of the rash: a negative early test does not cancel the suspicion.

steps.text: Never write 'await laboratory confirmation' as the next step. In notifiable disease questions that option is almost always wrong.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate action?' about who notifies (the suspecting doctor), to whom (UKHSA / local health protection team), how fast, whether consent is needed (it is not), and what happens to contacts.

points: The GP keeps Kofi out of the busy waiting room.
His mother asks: 'Do you have to tell anyone? I don't consent.'

steps.q: Who is legally responsible for notifying Kofi's measles?
steps.r: The **doctor who suspects** the disease has the legal duty, whoever confirms it later.

steps.lead: Kofi's GP phones the local health protection team (**UKHSA**) **immediately** because measles is urgent; no test result is awaited.

steps.text: Notification is a **statutory duty**: it does **not** need the patient's (or parent's) consent. Explain it kindly, but notify.

steps.lead: Kofi gets supportive care at home, is **isolated** from nursery, and the HPT traces his contacts: nursery, sister Ama, pregnant mother.

visual.title: Days since exposure (measles contacts)
visual.label: Ama: day 1
visual.caption: Early notification is what keeps contacts inside these windows.

steps.title: Contact management for measles
nodes: List contacts: home, nursery, waiting room
MMR within 72 h for susceptible contacts
Immunoglobulin for infants, pregnant and immunosuppressed contacts
steps.caption: Ama (5 months) and Abena (pregnant, check immunity) are the vulnerable contacts.

steps.title: Public health action after notification
head: Disease
Category
Contact action
rows: Contact screening; treat active TB ~6 months
Exclude food handlers until symptom-free 48 h

steps.lead: Kofi's GP follows the **Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010** and UKHSA guidance: report suspicion, urgent cases by phone.

steps.text: Who, what, when: the **suspecting clinician** notifies **UKHSA** (local HPT), **immediately** if urgent, otherwise **within 3 days**.

science.exam: Expect applied 'why' questions: why notify before confirmation, why some diseases are notifiable, and why measles or meningococcal disease are urgent while TB is routine.

steps.lead: Notifying Kofi on day 0 lets the HPT give Ama and the nursery protection **days before** the PCR result would have arrived.

steps.title: Why speed matters
nodes: Each case infects about 12 to 18 non-immune people
Post-exposure MMR only works within 72 h
steps.caption: Measles is one of the most contagious infections known.

steps.lead: Measles is chosen because it is highly **transmissible**, can cause pneumonia and encephalitis, and **MMR catch-up** for contacts works if given early.
Measles spreads fast with a short window for action, so it is **immediate**; TB spreads slowly, so a **3-day** window is safe.

steps.q: Why is TB routinely, not urgently, notifiable?
steps.r: TB spreads slowly with a long incubation, so the **3-day** window carries little added risk.

steps.text: Three filters make a disease notifiable: **transmissibility**, **severity** and **value of early intervention**.

mcq.r: Measles is urgent; TB, hepatitis B and food poisoning are routine (within 3 days).

mcq.q: Which of these is NOT legally notifiable in the UK?
mcq.r: **HIV** is monitored but not legally notifiable.

mcq.q: What is the typical treatment length for active TB?
mcq.r: Active TB is treated for about **6 months**.

mcq.q: When should a suspected notifiable disease be reported?
Which tests are done after notification to confirm the disease?
Who is legally responsible for notification?
mcq.r: The diagnosing or suspecting clinician, to UKHSA.

mcq.q: Within what time must a routine notifiable disease be reported?
What usually follows notification of an outbreak-prone disease?
mcq.r: The HPT traces contacts and offers vaccine or prophylaxis.

mcq.q: Why must measles be notified immediately?
mcq.r: Short incubation and high spread need immediate action.

glossary.notifiable disease: An infection that a doctor must legally report to public health authorities when it is suspected.
glossary.UKHSA: UK Health Security Agency, which replaced Public Health England and receives notifications.
glossary.HPT: Health protection team: the local UKHSA team that receives notifications and organises contact tracing.
glossary.health protection team: The local UKHSA team that receives notifications and manages outbreaks and contacts.
glossary.Public Health England: The former name of the national public health agency, replaced by UKHSA in 2021.
glossary.measles: A highly contagious paramyxovirus infection causing fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and a spreading rash.
glossary.Koplik spots: Tiny white spots on a red base inside the cheeks, seen early in measles.
glossary.coryza: Runny, blocked nose from inflammation of the nasal lining.
glossary.conjunctivitis: Red, watery, inflamed eyes; part of the measles prodrome.
glossary.rubella: German measles: a mild viral rash illness, dangerous to the fetus in pregnancy.
glossary.MMR: Combined live vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella; given at 1 year and 3 years 4 months.
glossary.immunoglobulin: Pooled antibodies given to vulnerable contacts for short-term passive protection after exposure.
glossary.post-exposure prophylaxis: Treatment or vaccine given after contact with an infection to stop the disease developing.
glossary.PEP: Post-exposure prophylaxis: preventive treatment given after an exposure.
glossary.prophylaxis: Treatment given to prevent disease rather than treat it.
glossary.contact tracing: Finding and advising everyone who was exposed to a case so they can be tested or protected.
glossary.meningococcal septicaemia: Bloodstream infection with Neisseria meningitidis, causing shock and a non-blanching rash.
glossary.Neisseria meningitidis: Gram-negative diplococcus that causes meningococcal meningitis and septicaemia.
glossary.non-blanching: A rash that does not fade when pressed with a glass; suggests bleeding into the skin.
glossary.purpuric: Describes purple spots from bleeding under the skin that do not blanch.
glossary.ciprofloxacin: A quinolone antibiotic given as a single dose to close contacts of meningococcal disease.
glossary.whooping cough: Pertussis: Bordetella pertussis infection with bouts of coughing and an inspiratory whoop.
glossary.pertussis: Whooping cough, caused by Bordetella pertussis; dangerous in unvaccinated young infants.
glossary.post-tussive vomiting: Vomiting straight after a coughing fit, typical of whooping cough.
glossary.cholera: Vibrio cholerae infection causing profuse rice-water diarrhoea; urgently notifiable.
glossary.rabies: A fatal viral encephalitis spread by animal bites; urgently notifiable.
glossary.food poisoning: Gut infection from contaminated food, e.g. Campylobacter or Salmonella; routinely notifiable.
glossary.Campylobacter: The commonest bacterial cause of food poisoning in the UK, often from poultry.
glossary.TB: Tuberculosis, a Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection; routinely notifiable.
glossary.hepatitis B: A blood-borne viral liver infection; routinely notifiable.
glossary.ophthalmia neonatorum: Conjunctivitis in a newborn's first month; recently removed from the notifiable list.
glossary.serology: Blood tests that detect antibodies (e.g. IgM, IgG) to an infection.
glossary.IgM: The first antibody made in a new infection; a positive IgM suggests recent infection.
glossary.IgG: The later, long-lasting antibody that shows past infection or immunity.
glossary.PCR: Polymerase chain reaction: detects the organism's genetic material, fast and sensitive.
glossary.oral fluid swab: A sponge rubbed along the gums to collect fluid for measles PCR and antibody tests.
glossary.blood cultures: Blood samples incubated to grow bacteria and identify the organism and its sensitivities.
glossary.statutory duty: A legal obligation set out in law; it does not depend on the patient's consent.
glossary.incubation period: The time between catching an infection and developing symptoms.
glossary.transmissibility: How easily an infection spreads from person to person.
glossary.outbreak: More cases of a disease than expected in a place or group over a time period.
glossary.isolation: Separating an infectious person from others to stop spread.

technique.stem: A 19 year old university student has a 12 hour history of fever, headache and vomiting. She now dislikes bright light and has a stiff neck. There is a non-blanching purpuric rash on her legs. She shares a flat with four other students.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question: put the headache, fever and rash together.
Meningism plus fever plus **non-blanching rash** = meningococcal disease. Shared housing matters for contacts.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Meningococcal meningitis: urgently notifiable, with prophylaxis for her flatmates.

elim: Measles has a prodrome of cough, coryza and conjunctivitis and a blanching maculopapular rash.
Migraine does not cause fever or a purpuric rash.
Sudden thunderclap headache, no fever or rash.
Viral meningitis is milder and does not cause a non-blanching rash.

steps.x: **B. Meningococcal meningitis.** Rule: fever + non-blanching rash = meningococcal until proven otherwise; notify immediately.

technique.stem: A 6 year old boy who has not had MMR has a 3 day history of fever, cough and red eyes, and today a red maculopapular rash that began behind his ears. The GP suspects measles and takes an oral fluid swab. The result will take 3 days.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Await the oral fluid result before notifying
Notify the health protection team now
Notify within 3 days if the result is positive

steps.x: 'Next step' with a test pending: the trap is waiting for it.
Classic measles in an unvaccinated child; the result is days away.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Notify on **clinical suspicion**, immediately, while the swab is processed.

elim: Notification is on suspicion; waiting loses the contact window.
Measles is urgent, and suspicion is enough.
No reason to repeat, and it delays everything.
IgG shows past immunity; it does not confirm acute infection or replace notification.

steps.x: **B. Notify now.** Rule: never wait for lab confirmation in a notifiable disease.

technique.stem: A foundation doctor in the emergency department suspects meningococcal septicaemia in a 22 year old man and starts intravenous ceftriaxone. The microbiology result will not be available until tomorrow. The patient's partner asks who will tell public health.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate action regarding notification?
o: Laboratory notifies; no clinician action needed
Partner is asked to contact UKHSA

steps.x: A 'who and when' notification question.

clues: will not be available until tomorrow
steps.x: The **suspecting** doctor, an **urgent** disease, result not back.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The FY doctor notifies UKHSA (local HPT) immediately on suspicion.

elim: The duty sits with the suspecting doctor, and suspicion is enough.
Labs report organisms too, but that does not replace the clinician's duty.
Meningococcal disease is urgent: immediately, not within 3 days.
Families do not notify; the clinician does.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: the suspecting clinician notifies; urgent means now.

technique.stem: A health protection team receives a phone notification of suspected meningococcal disease in a nursery worker on the same day she is admitted. Her household contacts are given ciprofloxacin that evening, 2 days before PCR confirms Neisseria meningitidis.
technique.q: Which best explains why notification is required before laboratory confirmation?
o: Makes treatment of the patient free

steps.x: A 'why' question about the purpose of notification.

clues: household contacts are given ciprofloxacin that evening
steps.x: Contacts protected 2 days before confirmation: that is the point.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Notification enables rapid public health action (prophylaxis, tracing) before lab confirmation.

elim: Notification is a report of suspicion, not a diagnostic test.
Notification has nothing to do with paying for care.
PCR is still done to confirm the organism.
Notification does not need consent.

steps.x: **A. Early prophylaxis of contacts.** Rule: the law exists for speed of public health action.

practice.stem: A 4 year old girl who has not received MMR has a 4 day history of fever, runny nose, cough and sore red eyes. Today a red blotchy rash appeared on her face and behind her ears and is spreading to her trunk. There are white spots on her buccal mucosa. Her temperature is 39.6°C, pulse rate 148 bpm and respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: The 3 Cs (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis), Koplik spots and a rash spreading from behind the ears are measles. Rubella is milder without Koplik spots.

steps.x: Diagnosis: fever and rash in a child.

clues: runny nose, cough and sore red eyes
white spots on her buccal mucosa
steps.x: Unvaccinated, the 3 Cs prodrome, rash spreading from behind the ears, **Koplik spots**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Measles, which must be notified immediately.

elim: Gives mouth ulcers and a vesicular rash on hands and feet, without conjunctivitis.
Rash appears as the fever settles, usually under 2 years.
Milder, with lymphadenopathy and no Koplik spots.
Sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue and sore throat, not coryza and conjunctivitis.

steps.x: **B. Measles.** Fever + rash + unwell = measles; notify immediately.

practice.stem: A 17 year old boy has a 10 hour history of fever, aching legs and cold hands. He has a non-blanching purple rash on his trunk and legs. He is drowsy but has no neck stiffness. His temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 132 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fever, shock and a non-blanching rash are meningococcal septicaemia, which can occur without neck stiffness. ITP and HSP do not cause shock.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a shocked, febrile teenager with a rash.
Early sepsis signs, **non-blanching rash**, hypotension. No meningism does not exclude it.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Meningococcal septicaemia (Neisseria meningitidis): urgently notifiable.

elim: Palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs in a well child, without shock.
Bruising and petechiae in a well child; platelets would be very low, no fever or shock.
Diffuse erythroderma that blanches, often tampon-related, not a purpuric rash.
No shock and no purpuric rash.

steps.x: **C. Meningococcal septicaemia.** Septicaemia can occur without meningitis.

practice.stem: A 7 week old unvaccinated boy has had a cough for 2 weeks. The coughing comes in long bouts that leave him red in the face, followed by a gasp and then vomiting. Between bouts he looks well. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 150 bpm, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Paroxysmal cough with a whoop and post-tussive vomiting in an unvaccinated infant is pertussis, a notifiable disease. Bronchiolitis gives constant distress with wheeze and crackles.

steps.x: Diagnosis: a cough pattern in a young infant.

clues: followed by a gasp and then vomiting
steps.x: Paroxysms, whoop, **post-tussive vomiting**, well between bouts, unvaccinated young infant.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Whooping cough (pertussis), notifiable and dangerous at this age.

elim: Coryza, wheeze and crackles with continuous distress, not well between paroxysms.
Barking cough and stridor in an older infant or toddler.
Chronic cough with failure to thrive and greasy stools, not paroxysms.
Sudden choking episode in a mobile toddler, not a 7 week old.

steps.x: **E. Whooping cough.** Paroxysms + whoop + vomiting + unvaccinated infant.

practice.stem: A GP reviews five new diagnoses made at the practice this week. She wants to know which one does not need to be reported under the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations. The diagnoses are a new positive HIV test, acute hepatitis B, pulmonary tuberculosis, measles and Campylobacter food poisoning.
practice.q: Which condition is not legally notifiable?
practice.e: HIV is monitored for public health purposes but is not legally notifiable. Hepatitis B, TB and food poisoning are routine; measles is urgent.

steps.x: A 'which is not notifiable' question: find the odd one out.

clues: does not need to be reported
steps.x: Recall the not-notifiable list: HIV, syphilis, herpes simplex, ophthalmia neonatorum.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: HIV is monitored but not legally notifiable.

elim: Routinely notifiable (within 3 days).
Food poisoning is routinely notifiable, even when it resolves.
Urgently notifiable.
Routinely notifiable.

steps.x: **C. HIV.** It is surveilled, not notified.

practice.stem: A 45 year old chef has 3 days of bloody diarrhoea, cramping abdominal pain and fever after a barbecue. He is improving with oral fluids. His stool culture has now come back.
practice.q: Which is the correct notification category for this condition?
o: Not notifiable because he is improving
Not notifiable unless there is an outbreak
Notifiable only with the patient's consent
practice.e: Food poisoning is routinely notifiable within 3 days, whatever the outcome; as a chef he must also be excluded from work until 48 hours symptom-free.

steps.x: Classify the disease first: food poisoning.
Campylobacter food poisoning in a food handler: notifiable, routine category.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Routine notification within 3 days (he also needs exclusion from food handling).

elim: That is for measles, meningococcal disease, cholera and rabies.
Recovery does not remove the legal duty.
A single case is notifiable.
Notification does not need consent.

steps.x: **E. Routine, within 3 days.** Food poisoning is routine; urgent is measles, meningococcal, cholera, rabies.

practice.stem: A 34 year old man who moved from Somalia 2 years ago has a 3 month history of cough, night sweats and 7 kg weight loss. He has coughed up blood twice. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Right upper zone consolidation with cavitation.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Chronic cough, night sweats, weight loss and haemoptysis with an upper zone cavity and acid-fast bacilli is pulmonary TB, a routinely notifiable disease.

steps.x: Diagnosis with a chest X-ray.

clues: night sweats and 7 kg weight loss
steps.x: High-incidence country, chronic course, B symptoms, haemoptysis, **upper zone cavity**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pulmonary TB, routinely notifiable.

elim: Daily copious sputum for years, not weight loss and night sweats over 3 months.
Acute illness over days, not months.
Possible, but a young man from a high-incidence country with night sweats and cavitation fits TB.
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, not an upper zone cavity.

steps.x: **D. Pulmonary TB.** Notify within 3 days; treat active disease for about 6 months.

practice.stem: A 20 year old woman is admitted with fever, a non-blanching rash and neck stiffness. Meningococcal disease is suspected and intravenous ceftriaxone has been given. The health protection team has been phoned.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the organism?
practice.e: Once notified, confirmatory tests follow: blood culture and meningococcal PCR, which stays positive after antibiotics have started.

steps.x: Confirming the organism after notification.

clues: health protection team has been phoned
steps.x: Already notified; now confirm. After antibiotics, cultures may be negative, so add **PCR**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Blood culture plus meningococcal PCR (which still works after antibiotics).

elim: Imaging does not identify the organism.
Not relevant to confirming meningococcus.
Measles is not suspected.
Meningococcus is bacterial; a viral swab will not confirm it.

steps.x: **A.** Rule: notify first, then confirm with cultures, PCR and serology.

practice.stem: A 28 year old unvaccinated teacher has a 4 day history of fever, cough and conjunctivitis and a maculopapular rash that started on her face today. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. The GP suspects measles.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Check measles IgG and notify if positive
Notify now and send oral fluid for PCR
Notify only if she develops complications
Send oral fluid for PCR and notify if positive
Wait for a second case at the school
practice.e: Measles is urgently notifiable on clinical suspicion; confirmatory oral fluid PCR is sent at the same time, never as a condition for notifying.

steps.x: A 'next step' with a suspected urgent disease.
Clinical measles in a teacher: many contacts.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Notify immediately on suspicion and send confirmatory samples in parallel.

elim: IgG shows immunity, not acute infection, and notification should not wait.
Complications are not a criterion; suspicion is enough.
Waiting for confirmation is the classic wrong answer.
One suspected case is enough.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: suspicion triggers notification; tests run alongside.

practice.stem: A 32 year old office worker sees her GP for the result of a stool test. It confirms Campylobacter food poisoning, which has fully resolved. The GP explains he must notify the health protection team. She refuses consent, saying she does not want her information shared.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate action?
o: Do not notify because she has recovered
Do not notify because she is not a food handler
Notify the health protection team without her consent
Refer to the practice's Caldicott guardian before notifying
practice.e: Notification is a statutory duty under the 2010 Regulations, so it does not need the patient's consent and must identify her so the team can follow up.

steps.x: A consent and confidentiality question about notification.
A statutory duty overrides refusal of consent; explain why to her.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Notify with identifiable details, explaining the legal requirement.

elim: Recovery does not remove the legal duty.
Her job affects exclusion advice, not the duty to notify.
Notification needs identifiable details so the team can follow up.
Unnecessary: the law already requires disclosure.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: notification is a legal duty; consent is not needed.

practice.stem: A 19 year old student is admitted to intensive care with meningococcal septicaemia and has been notified. His girlfriend stayed in his room the night before admission. She is well. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management for the girlfriend?
o: Throat swab and treat if positive
practice.e: Close contacts of meningococcal disease are given chemoprophylaxis, usually a single dose of ciprofloxacin, arranged with the health protection team after notification.

steps.x: Contact management after notification.

clues: stayed in his room the night before
steps.x: A close contact of meningococcal disease, well.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Antibiotic prophylaxis: single-dose ciprofloxacin.

elim: She is well; prophylaxis, not treatment, is needed.
MMR is for measles contacts.
Close contacts of meningococcal disease need prophylaxis.
Prophylaxis is given without waiting for swabs.

steps.x: **D. Ciprofloxacin.** Rule: notify, then trace and protect close contacts.

practice.stem: A foundation doctor on a respiratory ward diagnoses smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis in a 52 year old man. Culture and sensitivities will take several weeks. The patient is stable and isolated in a side room.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate action regarding notification?
o: Ask the patient's consent before notifying
Notify after culture confirms the diagnosis
Notify only if a contact becomes unwell
Notify the health protection team within 3 days
practice.e: TB is routinely notifiable: the diagnosing clinician notifies within 3 days without waiting for culture. The health protection team then screens contacts.

steps.x: A 'who, when' question for a routine disease.
TB is routinely notifiable; the diagnosing doctor notifies.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The doctor notifies within 3 days, without waiting for culture.

elim: Consent is not needed.
The suspecting clinician holds the duty.
Notify on suspicion; do not wait weeks.
TB is notifiable on its own.

steps.x: **E. Within 3 days.** TB is routine; urgent ones are phoned immediately.

practice.stem: A health protection consultant explains to medical students why measles must be notified by phone the same day it is suspected, whereas hepatitis B can be reported within 3 days. She points out that unvaccinated contacts of measles can be protected with MMR if given quickly.
practice.q: Which best explains the difference in time frames?
o: Measles spreads fast with a short window to protect contacts
practice.e: Highly transmissible, short-incubation diseases with time-critical interventions (MMR within 72 hours) need immediate notification; lower-risk diseases allow 3 days.
